ref: Haer. praefatio Book V (Harvey 'LIBER V. PRAEFATIO'; ANF 'Preface'). NOT 5.1.1 as in the brief
greek: Verbum Dei, Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum: qui propter immensam suam dilectionem factus est quod sumus nos, uti nos perficeret esse quod et ipse.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin, Harvey vol. II (PDF p.325). Brief's '5.1.1' is wrong: this sentence is the Book V preface. Preface Greek not located.
english: ...following the only true and steadfast Teacher, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: Harvey p. 313 (inferred: PDF 324 minus 11; head illegible); ANF page unknown
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: The Word of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, became what we are, so that we might become what he is.
limits: Names the Word only; no Spirit or Father in the sentence. 'propter immensam suam dilectionem' (ANF: 'transcendent love'). Does not show Nicene homoousios.

ref: Haer. 5.1.1 (Harvey V.1.1; ANF Book V ch.1 para 1)
greek: [Non] enim aliter nos discere poteramus quae sunt Dei, nisi magister noster, Verbum existens, homo factus fuisset. Neque enim alius poterat enarrare nobis quae sunt Patris, nisi proprium ipsius Verbum. Quis enim alius cognovit sensum Domini? aut quis alius ejus consiliarius factus est?
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin. OCR reads 'Now' for the first word; '[Non]' supplied by context. Greek of 5.1.1 not located (searched Harvey PDF 325-327).
english: For in no other way could we have learned the things of God, unless our Master, existing as the Word, had become man. For no other being had the power of revealing to us the things of the Father, except His own proper Word. For what other person knew the mind of the Lord, or who else has become His counsellor?
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: Only the Word, who became man, could reveal the Father's things; no one else knows the Lord's mind.
limits: Revelation by the Word, not an explicit Trinity. The Latin is 'Verbum existens' (existing as Word), not 'Verbum Dei' hypostasis language.

ref: Haer. 5.6.1 (Harvey V.vi.1; ANF Book V ch.6 para 1)
greek: Per manus enim Patris, id est, per Filium et Spiritum fit homo secundum similitudinem Dei, sed non pars hominis. [Latin, Harvey] | Greek (Eusebius, H.E. 5.7, as printed by Harvey, covers only the later sentence 'Quemadmodum et multos audivimus...'): Καθὼς καὶ πολλῶν ἀκούομεν ἀδελφῶν ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, προφητικὰ χαρίσματα ἐχόντων, καὶ παντοδαπαῖς γλώσσαις λαλούντων διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, καὶ τὰ κρύφια τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἰς φανερὸν ἀγόντων ἐπὶ τῷ συμφέροντι, καὶ τὰ μυστήρια τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκδιηγουμένων.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Greek is a partial Eusebian fragment; OCR columns reassembled in order (line order garbled in the layer), so check the Greek on the page image. Harvey footnote (p.333 n.): 'Another clear reference to the doctrine of the Ever-Blessed Trinity. The Son and Spirit are in the same way styled the Hands of the Father'.
english: For by the hands of the Father, that is, by the Son and the Holy Spirit, man, and not [merely] a part of man, was made in the likeness of God.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: Harvey p. 333 (Latin, running head read); Greek p. 334 (inferred)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: Man was made by the Father's two hands, the Son and the Holy Spirit, after God's likeness.
limits: 'hands' is a metaphor in Irenaeus; the Spirit is paired with the Son in creation. The Greek covers only part of the paragraph. Harvey's note is an editor's comment, not Irenaeus.

ref: Haer. 5.12.2 (Harvey V.xii.2; ANF Book V ch.12 para 2)
greek: Aliud enim est afflatus vitae, qui et animalem efficit hominem: et aliud Spiritus vivificans, qui et spiritalem efficit eum. ... Aliud autem est quod factum est, ab eo qui fecit. Afflatus igitur temporalis; Spiritus autem sempiternus. | Greek (Catena, as printed in Harvey): ἕτερον δέ ἐστι τὸ ποιηθὲν τοῦ ποιήσαντος. ἡ μὲν οὖν πνοὴ πρόσκαιρος, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ἀένναον
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Greek from a catena (Harvey's apparatus cites Halloix and a Genesis catena); Greek layer is OCR, polytonic accents as read; 'ἀένναον' may be OCR for ἀένναον/ἀέναον: verify on image.
english: For the breath of life ... is one thing, and the vivifying Spirit another ... The breath, then, is temporal, but the Spirit eternal. ... what has been made is a different thing from him who makes it.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: Harvey p. 351 (inferred: PDF 362 minus 11; OCR of head unreadable)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: The Spirit is eternal, unlike the created breath of life, which is temporal and a made thing.
limits: Irenaeus contrasts Spirit with creation; he does not say 'Spirit is God' in these words. Opponents can say the Spirit 'is poured out' (adoption) so is a gift. Sentence 'Spiritum autem proprie in Deo deputans' is the key.

ref: Haer. 5.17.4 (Harvey V.xvii.4; ANF Book V ch.17 para 4)
greek: Duae quidem manus, quia et duo populi dispersi in fines terrae: unum autem medium caput, quoniam et unus Deus super omnes, et per omnes, et in omnibus nobis. | Greek: Δύο μὲν γὰρ αἱ χεῖρες, ὅτι καὶ δύο λαοὶ διεσπαρμένοι εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς γῆς· μία δὲ μέση κεφαλή, ὅτι εἷς ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, καὶ διὰ πάντων, καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ἡμῖν.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Greek is OCR of the Harvey page (PDF 383), words in order; Harvey's Greek and Latin match. Irenaeus is quoting 'a certain man among our predecessors' (quidam de senioribus).
english: For these were two hands, because there were two peoples scattered to the ends of the earth; but there was one head in the middle, as there is but one God, who is above all, and through all, and in us all.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: Harvey p. 372 (inferred from PDF 383; head OCR '972')
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: The cross's two hands gather two peoples into one God, who is over all, through all and in us all.
limits: Names only one God (Father-style formula, Eph 4:6). Unitarians cite this as a 'one God' text. The Son and Spirit are not named in the sentence; the triad is not spelled out here. Quoted from an unnamed elder.

ref: Haer. 5.18.1 (Harvey V.xviii.1; ANF Book V ch.18 para 1); chapter heading Harvey CAP. XVIII
greek: Creaturas universas, quibus Deus Pater et ejus Verbum utuntur, sua, propria, virtute et sapientia, condiderunt; ... sed per ea quae ex sapientia et virtute Patris ejus substantiam habuerunt.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only for this paragraph (Greek of 5.18 not located). Chapter heading on PDF 383, text on PDF 384.
english: And such or so important a dispensation He did not bring about by means of the creations of others, but by His own; neither by those things which were created out of ignorance and defect, but by those which had their substance from the wisdom and power of His Father.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: God the Father and His Word made all things by their own power and wisdom, not by ignorant or defective agents.
limits: 'Wisdom and power of the Father' is an attribute, not a named Spirit. Passage is about creation against Gnostic demiurges, not about the Trinity as such.

ref: Haer. 5.18.2 (Harvey V.xviii.2; ANF Book V ch.18 para 2)
greek: Super omnia quidem Pater, et ipse est caput Christi: per omnia autem Verbum, et ipse est caput Ecclesiae: in omnibus autem nobis Spiritus, et ipse est aqua viva ... Pater enim conditionem simul et Verbum suum portans, et Verbum portatum a Patre praestat Spiritum omnibus, quemadmodum vult Pater.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only (no Greek located). Harvey footnote on PDF 384 (editor, not Irenaeus): 'The Holy Spirit therefore, proceedeth from the Father and the Son'.
english: ... The Father is indeed above all, and He is the Head of Christ; but the Word is through all things, and is Himself the Head of the Church; while the Spirit is in us all, and He is the living water ... one God the Father, who is above all, and through all, and in us all.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: Father above all and head of Christ; Word through all and head of the Church; Spirit in all, as living water.
limits: Explicit ordering (Father above, Word through, Spirit in), with 'Father is head of Christ'. Opponents read subordination; Trinitarians read it as ordering of economy. Harvey's footnote on procession is not Irenaeus. 'Word ... grants the Spirit ... as the Father wills' (5.18.2, Latin 'praestat Spiritum omnibus') is also used by subordinationists.

ref: Haer. 5.18.3 (Harvey V.xviii.3; ANF Book V ch.18 para 3)
greek: Mundi enim factor vere Verbum Dei est: hic autem est Dominus noster, qui in novissimis temporibus homo factus est, existens in hoc mundo.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only.
english: For the Creator of the world is truly the Word of God: and this is our Lord, who in the last times was made man.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: The Word of God is the Creator of the world and the Lord made man in the last times.
limits: Creation through the Word is the point; the Word is distinct from the 'Father' in the same paragraph. Not an explicit consubstantiality claim.

ref: Haer. 5.20.1 (Harvey V.xx.1; ANF Book V ch.20 para 1)
greek: ... omnibus unum et eundem Deum Patrem praecipientibus, et eandem dispositionem incarnationis Filii Dei credentibus, et eandem donationem Spiritus scientibus, et eadem meditantibus praecepta ... (Harvey apparatus: 'recipientibus' AB for praecipientibus)
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only; Harvey's apparatus records variants (praecipientibus/recipientibus). Harvey's footnote (PDF 389 n.) reads this as a summary of the 'Regula Fidei' / Creed.
english: ... since all receive one and the same God the Father, and believe in the same dispensation regarding the incarnation of the Son of God, and are cognizant of the same gift of the Spirit.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: The Church's faith is one: one God the Father, the incarnation of the Son of God, and the gift of the Spirit.
limits: A summary of the rule of faith (creedal shape), not a formula defining the Son or Spirit as God. Opponents say it is only 'one God the Father' with Son and Spirit as dispensations.

ref: Haer. 5.20.2 (Harvey V.xx.2; ANF Book V ch.20 para 2), end of paragraph
greek: ... adunans hominem spiritui, et spiritum collocans in homine, ipse caput spiritus factus est, et spiritum dans esse hominis caput: per illum enim videmus, et audimus, et loquimur.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only. Harvey PDF 391; a Greek parallel for this paragraph was not located.
english: ...by uniting man to the Spirit, and causing the Spirit to dwell in man, He is Himself made the head of the Spirit, and gives the Spirit to be the head of man. For through Him (the Spirit) we see, and hear, and speak.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: Christ, uniting man to the Spirit, is made head of the Spirit, and the Spirit is head of man.
limits: Hard passage: 'head of the Spirit' reads as the Son over the Spirit (subordination). Context is recapitulation and anthropology (man made spiritual), not ontological ordering. Defence (my reading of the context, not checked against a commentary): 'caput' is economic, not rank in being; the sentence itself is not explicit about the Spirit's nature.

ref: Haer. 5.28.4 (Harvey V.xxviii.4; ANF Book V ch.28 para 4)
greek: Et propter hoc in omni tempore, plasmatus initio homo per manus Dei, id est, Filii et Spiritus, fit secundum imaginem et similitudinem Dei, paleis quidem abjectis, quae sunt apostasia; frumento autem in horreum assumto, quod est hi qui ad Deum fide fructificant.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only for this sentence (Greek on PDF 414 covers the martyr quotation and 5.28.3, not 5.28.4 'manus').
english: man, having been moulded at the beginning by the hands of God, that is, of the Son and of the Spirit, is made after the image and likeness of God.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: Harvey p. 403 (inferred from PDF 414; head OCR '408')
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: Man is formed in every age by the hands of God, that is, the Son and the Spirit, after the image of God.
limits: Same 'hands' formula as 5.6.1; the Father is not named in this sentence, so it is not a full triad. Opponents say 'hands' are the Father's instruments (created intermediaries).

ref: Haer. 5.36.2 (Harvey V.xxxvi.2; ANF Book V ch.36 para 2), reporting the presbyters
greek: ... et per Spiritum quidem ad Filium, per Filium autem ascendere ad Patrem; Filio deinceps cedente Patri opus suum, quemadmodum et ab Apostolo dictum est: Quoniam oportet regnare eum, quoadusque ponat omnes inimicos sub pedibus ejus ... tunc ipse Filius subjectus erit ei, qui sibi subjecit omnia, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only for the ascent sentence; the Greek on PDF 439 is the sentence 'Omnia enim Dei sunt' only. Harvey notes the presbyter source (Presbyteri Apostolorum discipuli).
english: ... they ascend through the Spirit to the Son, and through the Son to the Father, and that in due time the Son will yield up His work to the Father ... then shall the Son also Himself be subject unto Him who put all things under Him, that God may be all in all.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: Irenaeus reports the presbyters' teaching: the saved ascend through the Spirit to the Son and through the Son to the Father; the Son finally yields the work to the Father (1 Cor 15:28).
limits: The three degrees are attributed to 'the presbyters, the disciples of the apostles', not stated in Irenaeus's own voice. The 'Son subject' (1 Cor 15:28, quoted in 5.36.2) sentences are the classic Arian and subordinationist text; defence: the subjection is of the Son's human work and economy, not of his being (answer given by later Nicene writers; not checked here).

ref: Haer. 5.36.3 (Harvey V.xxxvi.3; ANF Book V ch.36 para 3)
greek: Etenim unus Filius, qui voluntatem Patris perfecit; et unum genus humanum, in quo perficiuntur mysteria Dei ... ut progenies ejus primogenitus Verbum descendat in facturam, hoc est in plasma, et capiatur ab eo; et factura iterum capiat Verbum, et ascendat ad eum ... et fiet secundum imaginem et similitudinem Dei.
greek_edition: Greek/Latin read from Harvey vol. II text layer (OCR, not checked against the page image); Latin only (PDF 440; Harvey 'Explic. libri beat. S. Irenaei'). The Latin ends the book in Harvey.
english: ... For there is the one Son, who accomplished His Father's will; and in all these things, and by them all, the same God the Father is manifested ... the creature should contain the Word, and ascend to Him.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885 (New Advent HTML; no printed page numbers)
what_it_says: The one Son fulfils the Father's will; the Word descends into creation and the creature ascends to the Word; the same God the Father is shown in all.
limits: 'One Son who did the Father's will' is read by opponents as obedience/subordination; Irenaeus's wording is economic. Also the Latin 'primogenitus Verbum' phrase; the Greek is absent.

ref: ANF Fragments no. 8 = Harvey, Fragmenta VIII (Greek). Cited by Irenaeus as from 'the Pascha' book (Harvey)
greek: Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ κιβωτὸς κεχρυσωμένη ἔσωθεν καὶ ἔξωθεν χρυσίῳ καθαρῷ ἦν· οὕτω καὶ τὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ σῶμα καθαρὸν ἦν καὶ διαυγές· ἔσωθεν μὲν τῷ Λόγῳ κοσμούμενον, ἔξωθεν δὲ τῷ Πνεύματι φρουρούμενον· ἵνα ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων τὸ περιφανὲς τῶν φύσεων παραδειχθῇ. | Latin: Nam sicut arca (V. Testamenti) inaurata intus et foris auro puro erat: ita et Christi corpus purum erat ac splendidum; intus quidem Verbo ornatum, foris autem Spiritu communitum: ut ex ambobus naturarum splendor commonstraretur.
greek_edition: Harvey vol. II, Greek with Latin, printed p. 479 (PDF 490). OCR of Greek layer; Harvey apparatus notes variants (ὁ Χριστός, ἐπιδειχθῇ). Harvey's note: cited by Leontius as Irenaeus's, and in a Paris MS (Cod. 2951); 'the precise treatise ... may still remain in obscurity'.
english: For as the ark [of the covenant] was gilded within and without with pure gold, so was also the body of Christ pure and resplendent; for it was adorned within by the Word, and shielded without by the Spirit, in order that from both [materials] the splendour of the natures might be clearly shown forth.
translator: Alexander Roberts (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: ANF Fragments no. 8; printed page unknown
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / ANF vol. 1, 1885 (New Advent 0134.htm)
what_it_says: Christ's body is like the gilded ark: adorned within by the Word and guarded without by the Spirit.
limits: Not from Haer. or Dem.; transmitted in later citations (Leontius, a Paris MS, per Harvey). Harvey himself treats it as probably genuine. Its place in the treatise is unknown. Greek is OCR. Authenticity not independently checked.

ref: ANF Fragments no. 39 = Harvey, Fragmenta XXXVIII (Pfaff, from the Turin copy). Warning: Pfaff fragment, doubtful
greek: Χριστὸς ὁ πρὸ αἰώνων κληθεὶς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς ἐν τῷ πληρώματι τοῦ καιροῦ ὥφθη, ... (OCR). | Latin (Harvey): Christus ante secula vocatus Dei Filius in complemento temporis apparuit, ut nos, qui sub jugo peccati eramus, per sanguinem suum purificet, inculpatos Patri filios sistens, et castigationi spiritus obedientes nos praestemus.
greek_edition: Harvey vol. II, p. 506 (PDF 517), Greek OCR; Latin in Harvey's text. Harvey's note: copied by C. M. Pfaff from the Royal Library at Turin; 'the volume from whence it was taken has disappeared'.
english: Christ, who was called the Son of God before the ages, was manifested in the fullness of time, in order that He might cleanse us through His blood, who were under the power of sin, presenting us as pure sons to His Father, if we yield ourselves obediently to the chastisement of the Spirit. And in the end of time He shall come to do away with all evil, and to reconcile all things, in order that there may be an end of all impurities.
translator: Alexander Roberts (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: ANF Fragments no. 39; printed page unknown
edition: W. W. Harvey, Sancti Irenaei ... Libros quinque adversus haereses, vol. II, Cantabrigiae: Typis Academicis, 1857 (Google scan on archive.org, text layer) / ANF vol. 1, 1885 (New Advent 0134.htm)
what_it_says: Christ, called Son of God before the ages, appeared in the fullness of time to cleanse us by his blood.
limits: Pfaff fragment: source MS lost, provenance not verifiable; treat as doubtful. Harvey (p. 509 note) says it is impossible to tell which work it came from. Says 'Son of God before the ages' but no 'consubstantial'.

greek_edition: Original not located: searched Harvey vol. II Fragmenta (PDF 505-531) for Greek/Latin of 'sacred books' / Word / God; not found in Harvey 1857. Source Pfaff (Turin copy lost) per Harvey's note.
english: The sacred books acknowledge with regard to Christ, that as He is the Son of man, so is the same Being not a [mere] man; and as He is flesh, so is He also spirit, and the Word of God, and God. And as He was born of Mary in the last times, so did He also proceed from God as the First-begotten of every creature; and as He hungered, so did He satisfy [others]; and as He thirsted, so did He of old cause the Jews to drink, for the Rock was Christ 1 Corinthians 10:4 Himself: thus does Jesus now give to His believing people power to drink spiritual waters, which spring up to life eternal. John 4:14 And as He was the son of David, so was He also the Lord of David. And as He was from Abraham, so did He also exist before Abraham. John 8:58 And as He was the servant of God, so is He the Son of God, and Lord of the universe. And as He was spit upon ignominiously, so also did He breathe the Holy Spirit into His disciples. John 20:22 And as He was saddened, so also did He give joy to His people. [...]
translator: Alexander Roberts (ANF vol. 1, 1885; as revised on New Advent)
page: ANF Fragments no. 52; printed page unknown
edition: ANF vol. 1, 1885 (New Advent 0134.htm); Harvey 1857 searched, not found
what_it_says: The sacred books say Christ is Son of man, and also flesh, spirit, Word of God, and God.
limits: Doubtful Pfaff-type fragment; no original located; cannot be verified. Do not use as evidence for Irenaeus without another source.

greek_edition: Original not located in Harvey 1857 vol. II (searched PDF 505-531 for 'Deus in Deo', 'Intellectus', 'Verbum', Greek 'Νοῦς'); no source text read.
english: With regard to Christ, the law and the prophets and the evangelists have proclaimed that He was born of a virgin, that He suffered upon a beam of wood, and that He appeared from the dead; that He also ascended to the heavens, and was glorified by the Father, and is the Eternal King; that He is the perfect Intelligence, the Word of God, who was begotten before the light; that He was the Founder of the universe, along with it (light), and the Maker of man; that He is All in all: Patriarch among the patriarchs; Law in the laws; Chief Priest among priests; Ruler among kings; the Prophet among prophets; the Angel among angels; the Man among men; Son in the Father; God in God; King to all [...] ... The law and the prophets and evangelists have declared that Christ was born of a virgin, and suffered on the cross; was raised also from the dead, and taken up to heaven; that He was glorified, and reigns forever. He is Himself termed the Perfect Intellect, the Word of God.
